title: The Principal Grapes
description: The eight grapes behind most of the wine you'll ever be offered, and what each one tastes like.
L: Why the name of the grape tells you so much
Explain what a grape variety is
Explain how varieties are kept identical
Explain why a variety predicts a style

A grape variety is a distinct type of vine within Vitis vinifera, with its own berry size, skin thickness, acidity and aromas. Chardonnay, Merlot and Riesling are varieties. Knowing the variety tells you a lot about how the wine will taste before you open it.
Variety: a type of vine with its own character

A seed from a Chardonnay grape would grow into a new, different vine, because vines don't breed true. So growers plant cuttings, pieces of an existing vine, which are genetically identical to the parent. A Chardonnay vine in Chile is effectively a copy of one in Burgundy. Most vines today are also grafted onto American rootstocks to resist phylloxera, an insect that destroyed Europe's vineyards in the late 1800s.
Vines are copied by cuttings, not grown from seed
A vine grown from a Merlot seed will produce Merlot grapes.
Not true. Vines don't breed true from seed, so the seedling would be a new variety. That's why vineyards are planted with cuttings.

A varietal wine is made mainly from one variety and often names it on the label, like a Chilean Sauvignon Blanc. A blend mixes varieties for balance, like Bordeaux, which combines Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. In the EU and many other places, a wine that names one variety must contain at least 85% of it.
Varietal labels usually mean at least 85% of that grape
A Chilean label names only Cabernet Sauvignon. What can you expect?
It is 100% Cabernet Sauvignon by law
It is mostly Cabernet Sauvignon, possibly with a little of another grape
It is a blend with no main grape
It is Cabernet grown from seed
Naming one variety usually means at least 75 to 85% of it, depending on the country. A small share of another grape is allowed.
A variety is a type of vine with its own character
Vines are propagated by cuttings, so each variety stays identical
A varietal wine names the grape that makes up most of it
Two white grapes, two ways to be white
Explain why Chardonnay changes so much with winemaking

Chardonnay has a neutral character of its own, so it reflects where it grows and how it is made. In cool places like Chablis it tastes of green apple and lemon, lean and crisp. In warmer places it gives peach, pineapple and melon. It is also the main grape of many sparkling wines, including most Blanc de Blancs Champagne.

Sauvignon Blanc is intensely aromatic, with gooseberry, passion fruit, cut grass and green pepper. The green notes come from compounds called pyrazines, which survive best in cool climates. It is almost always made without oak to keep that freshness. Sancerre in France and Marlborough in New Zealand are its two best-known homes.
Sauvignon Blanc: grass, gooseberry, high acidity
Which aroma is most typical of Sauvignon Blanc?
Grassy and gooseberry aromas come from pyrazines and thiols in Sauvignon Blanc. Butter and toast come from oak and winemaking, as in some Chardonnays.

Because Chardonnay is neutral, it takes winemaking well. Oak barrels add vanilla, toast and spice. Malolactic conversion, where bacteria turn sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, gives a buttery note. Stirring the dead yeast, the lees, adds creaminess. Sauvignon Blanc rarely gets this treatment.
Oak, malolactic and lees shape Chardonnay
Match each flavour to its likely source.
Fruit comes from the grape and climate; butter, vanilla and toast come from the winery.
Chardonnay is neutral and reflects climate and winemaking
Sauvignon Blanc is aromatic, grassy and crisp, usually unoaked
Oak, malolactic and lees give Chardonnay toast, butter and cream
Describe Riesling's acidity and range of sweetness
Describe Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris
Explain how Riesling changes with age

Riesling comes from Germany and has very high acidity, flowery aromas and flavours from lime to peach. It is almost never oaked. It can be bone dry, as in much of Alsace and Austria, or lusciously sweet, as in German late-harvest wines. That acidity keeps even sweet Rieslings fresh.
Riesling: high acidity, dry to sweet

High acidity protects a wine as it ages. Good Riesling can develop for 20 years or more, gaining notes of honey, toast and a smell often called petrol. That petrol note comes from a compound called TDN, which forms more in grapes exposed to strong sun. Many lovers of Riesling look for it.
Petrol in Riesling comes from TDN
Riesling's ability to age comes mainly from its high ____.
Acidity acts as a preservative. Riesling has very little tannin and often modest alcohol, so acidity does the work.

Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the same grape, with a greyish-pink skin. The Italian name usually signals a light, crisp, neutral wine picked early, as in north-east Italy. The French name, from Alsace, usually means a riper, rounder wine with notes of pear, spice and honey. Producers elsewhere borrow the name to signal the style.
Grigio: light and crisp. Gris: rich and round.
A label says Pinot Gris and the wine comes from Alsace. Which style is most likely?
Rich and round, with ripe pear and spice
Pinot Gris from Alsace is usually riper and fuller. The Italian name, Pinot Grigio, is the one linked to the light, crisp style.
Riesling has high acidity and ranges from bone dry to sweet
Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are one grape, named by style
Good Riesling ages for decades, developing honey and petrol notes
Describe Cabernet Sauvignon's flavours and structure
Describe Merlot and how it differs
Explain why the two are often blended

Cabernet Sauvignon has small, thick-skinned berries, which give deep colour, high tannin and high acidity. Its flavours are blackcurrant and black cherry, with mint, cedar and sometimes green pepper. It ripens late, so it needs a warm site. Bordeaux's Médoc made it famous, and Napa Valley made it a star of the New World.

Merlot has bigger, thinner-skinned berries and ripens about two weeks earlier than Cabernet. Its tannins are softer and its flavours are plum, red and black cherry, with a rounder feel. It suits cooler, clay soils that would leave Cabernet unripe, as on Bordeaux's Right Bank in Pomerol and Saint-Émilion.
Merlot: plum, softer tannin, earlier ripening
Which grape is more likely to give a wine with firm tannin and blackcurrant aromas?
Cabernet's small, thick-skinned berries give more tannin, and blackcurrant is its signature aroma. Merlot is softer, more plum and cherry.

Cabernet brings structure and length; Merlot fills the middle with fleshy fruit. Together they make a more complete wine. Blending also spreads risk: if a cool year leaves Cabernet short of ripeness, Merlot, which ripens earlier, can make up the difference. That's the logic of most Bordeaux reds.
Cabernet gives the frame; Merlot fills it in
Which of these describe Merlot rather than Cabernet Sauvignon?
Merlot ripens earlier, is softer and plummy, and copes with cool clay. Thick skins, high tannin and blackcurrant are Cabernet's signature.
Cabernet Sauvignon gives blackcurrant, high tannin and acidity
Merlot gives plum and softer tannins, ripening earlier
Blending them balances structure and fruit, and spreads risk
Describe Pinot Noir's style and its demands
Tell the two apart by colour and flavour

Pinot Noir has thin skins, so it gives pale, low-tannin reds with red cherry, raspberry and, with age, earthy and mushroom notes. It needs a cool climate; in heat it loses its delicacy. It is fragile in the vineyard, prone to rot and sensitive to frost. Burgundy is its home, and it is also a key grape of Champagne.
Pinot Noir: pale, red fruit, cool climate

Syrah is a thick-skinned grape from the northern Rhône, giving deep colour, firm tannin and flavours of blackberry, black pepper and smoked meat. In Australia it is called Shiraz, and the warmer climate of places like the Barossa gives riper, sweeter fruit, chocolate and more alcohol. The pepper note comes from rotundone, more common in cooler sites.
Syrah: black fruit and black pepper
Syrah and Shiraz are two different grape varieties.
Not true. They are the same grape. The name often hints at style: Syrah for a cooler, peppery wine, Shiraz for a riper, fuller one.
Hold the glass over a white page. If you can read print through a red wine, you're likely looking at Pinot Noir or another thin-skinned grape. If it's nearly opaque, think Syrah or Cabernet.
A red is pale, with raspberry and a light earthiness, and gentle tannin. Which grape is most likely?
Pale colour, red fruit and low tannin point to Pinot Noir. Syrah, Shiraz and Cabernet are all deeply coloured and more tannic.
Pinot Noir is pale, low in tannin and needs a cool climate
Syrah gives deep colour, black fruit and pepper; in Australia it's Shiraz
Colour and tannin help you tell the two apart
Explain how climate changes a grape's flavour
Compare cool and warm climate versions of one grape
Predict style from a grape and a place

Climate is the long-term pattern of a place. In a cool climate, grapes ripen slowly, keeping high acidity and giving lighter body and fresher, sometimes green, fruit. In a warm climate, grapes ripen fully, with more sugar, lower acidity and flavours of ripe or even jammy fruit.
Cool: fresh, tart. Warm: ripe, full.

As grapes ripen, sugar rises and acidity falls. Heat speeds both up, and warm nights let the vine burn off malic acid, one of the grape's main acids. That's why a Chardonnay from Chablis may have 12% alcohol and sharp acidity, while one from a hot valley might reach 14.5% with soft acidity and tropical fruit.
Heat raises sugar and burns off acid
A Chardonnay is lean, with green apple and 12% alcohol. Where does it most likely come from?
Green apple, high acidity and moderate alcohol are signs of slow ripening in a cool place. A hot valley would give riper fruit and more alcohol.
The grape and the place together

Read a label as two clues. The grape tells you the basic character: aromas, skin, tannin. The place tells you how ripe it got. Sauvignon Blanc from the cool Loire tastes of grass and citrus; from warmer parts of Chile it leans towards passion fruit and melon. Same grape, different sun.
Grape gives character; place gives ripeness
Which are signs of a warm-climate wine?
Heat gives more sugar, so more alcohol and riper fruit, and it lowers acidity. Sharp acidity is a cool-climate sign.
Cool climates give fresher, lighter wines; warm ones riper and fuller
Heat raises sugar and lowers acidity
Grape gives the character, place gives the ripeness
Recognise the eight principal grapes by their flavours
Explain how varieties are propagated and labelled
Predict a wine's style from grape and climate
Match each grape to a typical aroma.
Each grape has a signature you can learn to recognise.
Why are vineyards planted with cuttings rather than seeds?
Vines don't breed true from seed
A seedling would be a new variety. Cuttings keep every vine identical to the parent.
Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the same grape.
Yes. The Italian name usually signals a light, crisp style; the French name a richer, rounder one.
Which grapes are normally deeply coloured and tannic?
Cabernet and Syrah have thick skins. Pinot Noir is pale and low in tannin, and Riesling is white.
Merlot ripens ____ than Cabernet Sauvignon, which helps in cooler years.
Merlot ripens about two weeks earlier, so it is the safer half of a Bordeaux blend in a cool year.
Eight grapes cover most wine: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Pinot Grigio, Cabernet, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Syrah
Varieties are copied by cuttings and named on varietal labels
Grape gives the character; climate gives the ripeness
